lead: A position encoder turns displacement into a digital number. An incremental encoder sends pulses; counting them gives how far a shaft or slide moved. An absolute encoder gives a full code at every position, correct as soon as power comes on. Output is already digital, so no ADC is needed, the value does not drift along the cable, and a microcontroller reads it directly. CNC machines, printer paper feeds, robot joints and servo motors use encoders.
prereq: You need resolution from the static characteristics of sensors and the idea of an interrupted light beam from photoelectric transducers.

sections.h3: Incremental encoders: channels A, B and Z

blocks.text: A rotary incremental encoder is a disc with N slots at equal angles, spinning between a light-emitting diode (LED) and a photodetector. Light through a slot makes the detector conduct; the solid part blocks light. The detector current becomes a square wave with N pulses per revolution.

A second track B has windows a quarter of a slot pitch ahead of track A, so B leads A by 90° of the pulse cycle. A third track, the index or Z channel, has one window and gives one pulse per revolution.

A linear scale works the same way. A glass or steel rule carries a grating with pitch p, the distance between lines, often 20 µm. The read head slides along it and produces the same A and B pulses. To use an incremental encoder: count pulses from A and B; bring the shaft to the Z pulse once at start-up to fix mechanical zero; multiply count by resolution to get displacement.

blocks.where: p is grating pitch in µm on a linear scale (or slot pitch in degrees on a rotary disc); the answer carries the same unit as p, per count: µm per count for a linear scale, degrees per count for a rotary one. For p = 20 µm, resolution = 5 µm.

sections.h3: Quadrature decoding: four counts per slot

blocks.text: Channels A and B are two square waves 90° apart. As a two-bit code the pair walks through 00 → 01 → 11 → 10 → 00. Four edges occur per slot, so a decoder counting every edge gets four counts per slot: ×4 or full quadrature decoding.

Read downwards, the table shows B leading A and the counter adds one. With opposite rotation A leads B, the same four states appear in reverse order, and the counter subtracts one. The controller knows distance and direction.

items: Sample A and B together on every clock tick, so both are read at the same instant.
Compare the pair with the pair from the previous tick to find which edge occurred.
Add 1 or subtract 1 from the position counter according to the direction of that edge.
On power-up, run the axis to the Z pulse and load the counter with zero.

blocks.text: counts per revolution = 4N; linear: counts per millimetre = 4/p
blocks.where: N is slots per revolution; 4 is the four edges per slot. For linear scales, counts per millimetre = 4/p with p in millimetres (p = 20 µm = 0.02 mm gives 200 counts/mm).
resolution is the smallest angle one count represents, in degrees; N is slots per revolution; 360° is one full turn.

sections.h3: Absolute encoders: binary, Gray code, magnetic and optical

blocks.text: An absolute encoder has n concentric tracks on one disc, each read by its own LED and photodetector. The n-bit word read in parallel is different for every position, giving 2ⁿ positions. No counting and no homing: position is on the wires immediately.

Plain binary code has a flaw. Going from 0111 to 1000, all four bits must change together. If the track edges are not perfectly aligned, or the read head is slightly tilted, the four bits do not switch at exactly the same angle, and the head can read 1111 for a moment: a false jump of eight positions. Gray code fixes this: only one bit changes between neighbouring positions, so the worst boundary error is one count.

The table in Figure 4.7.1 lists the 3-bit Gray code: each row differs from the row beside it in exactly one bit, and the last row (100) differs from the first (000) in one bit too, so the code also wraps round the disc. Software converts the Gray word to binary, then to an angle, by repeated exclusive-OR from the most significant bit down.

Construction splits into two types. Optical encoders give high resolution on servo motors and CNC axes. Magnetic encoders magnetise a drum in a coded pattern and read it with Hall sensors (see Hall effect sensors); they cost less and survive dust, oil and vibration, so they suit machine tools and vehicle steering.

blocks.where: θ<sub>res</sub> is smallest angle one code word represents, in degrees; n is the number of tracks; 2ⁿ is the number of positions per revolution.

items: Incremental: few wires, cheap, very high resolution; count is lost at power-off and needs homing.
Absolute: position survives power-off, no homing; more wires, higher cost.
Optical: fine pitch, high resolution; needs clean dry environment.
Magnetic: coarser but sealed and rugged; works in coolant spray and dust.

examples.question: A rotary incremental encoder has 1000 slots per revolution and is decoded with full quadrature (×4). (a) Find the counts per revolution. (b) Find the resolution in degrees per count. (c) How many counts are produced when the shaft turns through 90°?
steps: Given: N = 1000 slots per revolution, and full quadrature decoding counts four edges per slot.
(c) Counts for 90° = 90° / 0.09° = 1000 counts. Equivalently, 90° is one quarter of a turn, and 4000/4 = 1000 counts.
examples.answer: The encoder gives 4000 counts per revolution, a resolution of 0.09° per count, and 1000 counts for a 90° turn.
examples.check:
slots = 1000
counts = 4 * slots
res = 360 / counts
angle = 90
n = angle * counts / 360
print(counts)
print(res)
print(n)

examples.question: A linear scale has a grating pitch of 40 µm and is read with ×4 quadrature decoding. Find the resolution in µm, and the number of counts for a 25 mm travel.
steps: Resolution = p / 4 = 40 / 4 = 10 µm per count = 0.01 mm per count.
examples.answer: The resolution is 10 µm (0.01 mm) per count and the travel of 25 mm gives 2500 counts.
examples.check:
p = 40
res = p / 4
travel_um = 25 * 1000
print(res)
print(travel_um / res)

traps: Counting only channel A gives one quarter of the available resolution and no direction at all — the examiner's favourite question.
Resolution is not accuracy: the slot pitch sets resolution, but disc eccentricity, mounting tilt and bearing play set the true accuracy.
Raw Gray code is not a number. Reading a Gray word as if it were binary gives a wrong position; convert Gray to binary by XOR first.
Unit slip on linear scales: a 20 µm pitch with ×4 gives 5 µm per count, not 20 µm. Divide, do not stop at the pitch.
An incremental encoder loses its count when power fails; on restart the axis must be homed on the Z pulse before any position reading is trusted.

quiz.q: What is the index or Z channel of an incremental encoder?
quiz.a: A single-window track that produces exactly one pulse per revolution, used to set the mechanical zero position during homing.

quiz.q: Why does Gray code give an error of at most one count at a boundary, while binary code can give a large false jump?
quiz.a: In Gray code only one bit changes between neighbouring positions, so a misread boundary can differ from the true code by one step. In binary code several bits change together; if the tracks are slightly skewed the head can read a word that is far from the true position.

quiz.q: An absolute rotary encoder has 10 tracks. Find the number of positions per revolution and the resolution in degrees.
A 4-track Gray-code encoder reads 1101. Convert it to binary and find the shaft angle.
quiz.a: Binary bit b<sub>3</sub> = g<sub>3</sub> = 1; b<sub>2</sub> = b<sub>3</sub> ⊕ g<sub>2</sub> = 1 ⊕ 1 = 0; b<sub>1</sub> = b<sub>2</sub> ⊕ g<sub>1</sub> = 0 ⊕ 0 = 0; b<sub>0</sub> = b<sub>1</sub> ⊕ g<sub>0</sub> = 0 ⊕ 1 = 1. Binary 1001 = 9. Resolution 360°/2⁴ = 22.5°, so the angle is 9 × 22.5° = 202.5° (the start of position 9).

quiz.q: A robot joint uses an incremental encoder. The robot is switched off, the arm is pushed by hand, and power returns. What must the controller do before it can trust the joint angle, and why?
quiz.a: The pulse counter has lost the count, so the controller must drive the joint slowly to the Z pulse and reload the counter with zero (homing) before any angle is valid. The homing move should use a safe speed and a limit switch to avoid a collision.

quiz.q: Give one reason to choose a magnetic encoder and one reason to choose an optical encoder.
quiz.a: Magnetic: sealed against dust, oil and coolant, cheap, rugged, so it suits machine tools and vehicles. Optical: finer pitch and much higher resolution, so it suits servo motors and CNC axes in a clean environment.

quiz.q: A linear scale with pitch 20 µm uses ×4 decoding and has moved 8 mm from zero. How many counts should the counter hold?
quiz.a: Resolution = 20/4 = 5 µm = 0.005 mm per count. Counts = 8 mm / 0.005 mm = 1600 counts.

quiz.q: An incremental encoder with 500 slots per revolution is read by counting channel A only. State the resolution obtained and one consequence for a positioning system.
quiz.a: Counting A alone gives one count per slot, so resolution = 360°/500 = 0.72° instead of 360°/2000 = 0.18°. The system also cannot tell direction, so a shaft that reverses is counted wrongly and the position drifts.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industrial encoders may send position over serial links such as SSI, BiSS and EnDat, so one cable carries clock, data and error bits. Sine/cosine outputs are interpolated in software for fine resolution. Resolver-to-digital converters do the same job for rugged resolvers. Battery-backed multiturn counters remember full turns after a power cut. Search for 'quadrature decoder', 'Gray code to binary conversion', 'SSI encoder timing' and 'resolver-to-digital converter'.
